---
title: "Is this study ready to write up?"
---

**Pause point:** After the study and its main analyses, before drafting the account that others will rely on.

**Prevents:** Writing from memory, smoothing over deviations, overstating ambiguous results, or losing the connection between the research record and the reported claim.

**Use:** Do-confirm.

## Critical checks

- [ ] The study's actual question, evidence and contribution can be stated without relying on the preferred conclusion.
- [ ] The design, data, analysis and proposed claims are aligned at the same level of inference.
- [ ] Confirmatory, amended, exploratory, null, ambiguous, unexpected and sensitivity results are distinguished accurately.
- [ ] The final protocol, approvals, input-data reference, analysis record and deviations are available while writing.
- [ ] A suitable reporting guideline or disciplinary standard has been identified where one exists.
- [ ] Material limitations, missingness, uncertainty and contradictory evidence have been identified before drafting the discussion.
- [ ] Tables, figures, quotations and numerical results can be traced back to checked source material.
- [ ] The relationship between this study and other thesis studies is explicit, including overlap and dependence.
- [ ] Authorship, contributor roles and review responsibilities have been discussed before the draft becomes difficult to disentangle.
- [ ] Scope boundaries are recorded: what the study shows, what it does not show and what remains unresolved.

## Stop condition

Pause if the preferred account cannot be reconciled with the study record, material deviations or contradictory findings.

## Evidence to retain

Keep the reporting checklist, claim-evidence map, verified tables and figures, deviation record, contributor discussion and the version used for substantive review.
